Boot mismatch has no denial path (F3), but the specification assigns that check to the child and no child implementation exists in the repository; that is an incomplete scenario, not a false claim.

findings.summary: The invocation socket is listening before spawn, but the 'connection' handler is attached only after the durable append resolves. A child that connects inside that window is dropped silently by Node, the handshake is never served (spurious HANDOFF_SETUP_TIMEOUT and startupValid=false), and the orphaned accepted connection then prevents removeHandoffRuntime's server.close() from ever calling back, so runExitRetainingExecutor never returns.
findings.whyItMatters: Measured, not inferred: a probe with a 60 ms appendInvocationEvent and an immediate child connect gives servedHandshake=false, clientGotBytes=false and no return after 8 s; delaying the connect by 40 ms gives a normal HANDSHAKE_OK and a normal return. A separate probe confirms net.Server.close() never fires its callback while an accepted-but-unlistened socket is open, and that a connection emitted before the listener is attached is lost. The window is exactly the durable fsync, the slowest operation in the sequence, and the child's first act after reading its two environment values is to connect. The specification bounds every phase (cleanup, durable result and acknowledgment by outer+1740) and requires the wallet lock to be released after validated durable containment; an unbounded await in cleanup means the debit, claim and lock stay unresolved with no deadline, and a correct child is refused startup.

findings.summary: The commit states that the executor caller, fault matrix and prover-lifetime model are carried byte-identical from the approved round. fault-matrix and prover-lifetime (both modules and both tests) are byte-identical to the approved cff5f1e3. executor-caller.mjs and executor-caller.test.mjs are not: 2d61473270494654 -> ac87dccb3495154e and 4d53e804ef477b3b -> c85f0ff9009b578d.
findings.whyItMatters: The audit brief repeated the claim and instructed the auditor not to re-audit those files. The only high-severity defect found (F1) lives in exactly the code the claim excluded: a new validated option group, a new 21-field handoff contract, the socket/spawn ordering and the cleanup path. The change itself was necessary and is an improvement over the approved placeholder; the inaccuracy is in the provenance statement, which suppressed review of new code.

findings.summary: Boot mismatch, and the rest of the child's obligations (canonical payload digest against the store event, monotonic deadline, all current claim identities, same-UID private socket ownership), exist only as a comparator or not at all. No child implementation exists in the repository, so no boot mismatch can produce a denial.
findings.whyItMatters: The scenario requires all seven cases to deny or to yield the specified unknown cleanup outcome. Six have a real path in the parent; boot mismatch has none, and its dedicated test restates the assertions already made in test 10. Task 5.2 cannot be called complete for the scenario until either the child side exists in the model or the obligation is explicitly deferred with the specification amended to say so.

findings.summary: Ancestry is anchored on caller-supplied launcherPid and launcherStartTicks. The process this runner actually spawned is recorded as parentPid/parentStartTicks from a live /proc read but is never required to appear in the peer's chain; in the fixture the peer's chain (500 -> 400) never contains the spawned PID 4321.
findings.whyItMatters: Specification line 32 requires all payload identities to come from current validated producer state rather than caller assertions, and line 34 requires ancestry under the actual Foreman launcher with PID reuse and siblings denied. As wired, a same-UID process descended from the asserted launcher but not from this invocation's spawn satisfies the gate, and a stale or mistaken launcherPid silently relocates the anchor. Retained start ticks are compared only at the anchor, so only the anchor's identity is reuse-proof. No test pins any relationship between the spawned child and the ancestry anchor.

findings.summary: The replay test's ordering assertion (record-start, record-done, denial-received) passes even when the implementation writes the denial bytes first and awaits the durable record afterwards (mutation M20), and even when the record is fire-and-forget (M2). A setImmediate-based recorder always resolves before socket data reaches the client, so the assertion cannot observe the reversal.
findings.whyItMatters: The orchestrator's judgement that the replay fix is genuine is correct on every other count, but its ordering leg rests on an assertion that cannot fail for the property it names. The ordering is nevertheless real at invocation-handoff.mjs:73 by construction. To make the assertion load-bearing the injected recorder must resolve only after an observable I/O turn (for example after an awaited socket round trip or a timer), not a microtask-adjacent setImmediate.

findings.summary: The caller-level consequences of a denial and of parent disappearance are untested, and parentLost cannot change any outcome: every matrix built in runPrepared carries terminalEvidencePersisted:false, which the fault matrix consumes before it reaches parentLost. Mutations M23 (ignore the denial) and M24 (drop the parent-loss classification) leave all 53 tests passing.
findings.whyItMatters: The scenario's requirement that a denial refuse startup without another debit or launch, and that parent disappearance yield the specified unknown cleanup outcome, are asserted nowhere end to end. STARTUP_INVALID is reachable and merely untested; PARENT_LOST is unreachable from this caller, so the wiring is currently decorative.

findings.summary: The cap of start+1800 by the fixed block deadline is never exercised: every fixture passes blockDeadlineMonotonicNs:null, and mutation M26 (always uncapped) survives both suites.
findings.whyItMatters: Specification line 32 makes the cap mandatory, and the deadline requirement forbids squeezing out the retained margin. An uncapped outer deadline would let the invocation plan past a block deadline with no test objecting.

findings.summary: Exactly-one-handshake is enforced across connections but only silently across lines: after the first line the data handler returns early, so a second handshake line on the same accepted socket receives no denial and no durable record. Mutation M32 (answer every line) survives all 28 tests.
findings.whyItMatters: The specification keeps the authenticated channel open through cleanup, so a second request on the live channel is the cheapest replay attempt available to a buggy or hostile child. The current behaviour is safe (no second payload is sent) but unobservable, which is the same defect class the first round was sent back for.

findings.summary: Denial codes are taken verbatim from the injected dependency's error message, and the four distinct pre-response predicates the specification names (current store event, active runtime reservation, master one-shot claim, held wallet ownership) collapse into a single opaque confirmCurrentState hook.
findings.whyItMatters: What the module enforces is ordering, not identity: any of the four can be silently absent from the caller's hook and the handshake still answers. The denial vocabulary is also unvalidated, so a dependency can emit a code that impersonates a different case in the durable denial record.

findings.summary: Four checks are implemented but unexercised: the response digest binding to the recorded invocation digest (M17 survives), durable recording of socketless denials such as EOF before setup and setup timeout (M28 survives), the randomness of the runtime directory suffix (M31 survives), and the parent /proc stat retry loop (M29 survives).
findings.whyItMatters: Each is a real safety property of the code; none would be missed by the suite if it were removed in a later refactor. The response digest binding in particular is what stops the parent from answering with a payload whose digest differs from the one already durably recorded.

findings.summary: removeRuntime failures are swallowed by an empty catch, so a socket or directory that could not be removed leaves no retained fact in the returned record.
findings.whyItMatters: The specification requires unresolved ownership to be retained rather than discarded; a silently failed cleanup of the runner's own runtime directory is exactly such a fact.

findings.summary: Peer UID and PID come from mandatory injected callbacks because Node exposes no SO_PEERCRED; the module declares this in its header, offers peerCredentialsUnavailable() as a loud default, and makes both hooks required options at every layer, so nothing silently passes. Separately, the requirement's obligation to establish by source inspection and an actual isolated launcher test that the pinned Foreman launcher inherits the two variables through strong containment is not discharged anywhere in this commit.
findings.whyItMatters: The peer-credential injection is honest and correctly fail-loud, but it means the peer UID gate is only as real as the future production wiring. The launcher-inheritance evidence is a source-approval precondition in the specification text, not an optional extra; the scenario permits a fake launcher for the protocol test, but the transport assumption remains unverified.

findings.summary: Authority equality uses a plain string comparison while the nonce uses timingSafeEqual, and the socket exists briefly at its umask-derived mode between bind and the chmod to 0600.
findings.whyItMatters: Both are defensible: the authority digest is a public digest rather than a secret, and the socket sits inside a directory created 0700 and re-chmodded 0700, so no other user can traverse to it in the window. Recorded so that a later reader does not mistake either for an oversight.

overreach.weakenedTests: none. executor-caller.test.mjs is purely additive (3 new tests, no existing assertion touched). In the handoff suite the round-one test already demanded {denied:'HANDOFF_REPLAY_DENIED'} and already failed the peer close with an explicit assert.fail; round two changed the implementation to deliver that denial after the peer's write and added assertions (durable denial record, event ordering, exactly-one confirm and response). The expectation was raised, never relaxed.

orchestratorJudgementOnReplayFix.reasoning: The denial comes from the one-shot guard alone (invocation-handoff.mjs:78 is the sole producer of HANDOFF_REPLAY_DENIED, and mutations M1 and M18 each fail exactly the replay test). The round-one defect was in the implementation, not the test: round one already sent a denial but wrote it synchronously on 'connection' before reading, so the client's in-flight write hit EPIPE; round two waits for the peer's first data, end or close before recording and answering. The durable record genuinely precedes the answer at invocation-handoff.mjs:73 and, for the invocation event, at executor-caller.mjs:104. The one correction to the orchestrator's reading is F5: the test's ordering assertion is satisfied by event-loop scheduling and survives a deliberate reversal, so that leg of the confidence comes from the code, not the test.
